newsitem.title: USA: U.S. reserves judgment on Russia-Belarus merger.
newsitem.headline: U.S. reserves judgment on Russia-Belarus merger.

text.p: The United States reserved judgment on Tuesday on Moscow's suggestions of a merger between Russia and Belarus and said any such border change would have to reflect the will of the people, not just the governments.

Russian President Boris Yeltsin made the proposal for a referendum on unity between the two Slav neighbours through a spokesman on Monday. Commentators suggested it was a move to counter NATO expansion plans, which Moscow and Minsk oppose.
Burns said the United States had not been apprised formally of Yeltsin's proposal by either Russia or Belarus but only knew of it through news reports.
"We need to know a lot more about what is in store here, what they have in mind, what the time table might be, what this union might represent," Burns told reporters.

"As you know, we certainly believe that any kind of change of borders, any kind of integration between states in that part of the world or any part of the world ought to reflect the will of the people. Not just the will of the governments involved, the will of the people," he said.
But Burns said in the case of Belarus, "it's a little bit difficult to assess the will of the people."

"I'm not really sure what the people are thinking. So we're going to reserve judgment on this. We're going to try to find out what the facts are. And then at the appropriate time, if in fact, this does go forward -- I don't know if it will or not -- then we'll perhaps be in a position -- better position to assess it," he added.

Belarus's new foreign minister, Ivan Antonovich, on Tuesday played down Yeltsin's call to speed up plans to merge the two countries but said his government would move ahead with integrating the two economies.
He had little enthusiasm for Yeltsin's proposed plebiscite. "Perhaps it's time to take a rest from referendums," he said.
Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko secured greatly expanded powers in last November's referendum and subsequently dissolved parliament, replacing it with a legislature packed with his supporters.
He has rejected criticism of his authoritarian rule, including a public rebuke in December at a summit of the the more than 50 nations in the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe.
